title: Solar Orbiter: Exploring the Sun-heliosphere connection. Definition Study Report
short_title: Solar Orbiter Definition Study Report (Red Book, 2011)
organisation: European Space Agency (Solar Orbiter Study Science Team, Project Team and industrial study team led by Astrium UK)
status_notes: The 'Red Book' prepared for mission adoption, dated July 2011 on the cover (PDF p. 1). It describes the January 2017 launch scenario; Solar Orbiter actually launched on 10 February 2020, so trajectory dates and some design values differ from the flown mission.
summary:
ESA's definition study report for Solar Orbiter, written before mission adoption, when launch was planned for January 2017. Chapters 2 to 4 set out the science questions, the measurement requirements and the ten-instrument payload. Chapter 5 covers the baseline trajectory with Venus resonances, the spacecraft design, configuration, system budgets, technical challenges and the radiation environment. Chapter 7 describes the ground segment and science operations, and chapter 8 the management.

For the OPEN-SPACE-INFO simulator the report is the source of the engineering anchors. The solar array is sized to deliver 974 W at a worst-case aphelion of 1.47 au, against a 919 W hibernation demand at 630 W/m2. The payload receives 180 W at a regulated 28 V. The downlink requirement is 150 kbit/s at 1 au to the 35 m Malargüe antenna, with daily 9-hour passes in the nominal phase. The solid-state mass memory stores up to 549 Gbit. Four reaction wheels are off-loaded with 10 N thrusters, and the solar arrays tilt about their long axis to limit cell temperature at perihelion, where the flux reaches about 13 times its 1 au value. Remote sensing is planned in three 10-day windows per orbit, centred on perihelion and on the latitude extremes.

key_points.text: Mission summary: three-axis stabilised platform, heat shield, two adjustable two-sided solar arrays; 150 kbit/s downlink at 1 au spacecraft-Earth distance; Malargüe 35 m antenna, 4 to 8 hours per day effective.

The solid-state mass memory stores up to 549 Gbit (823 Gbit with the redundant bank); four reaction wheels are complemented by 10 N thrusters used for safe mode, wheel off-loading and manoeuvres (§5.3.6).

The solar array, based on the BepiColombo MPO design, supplies 974 W at the worst-case aphelion of 1.47 au; the PCDU uses a maximum power point tracker and a regulated 28 V main bus; a lithium-ion battery (§5.3.6).
The solar-radiation-pressure torque profile, influenced by the solar-array tilt direction, determines the frequency of wheel off-loading (§5.4.1).
The HGA may need to be stowed in the shadow of the heat shield during close perihelion passages (§5.4.1).
Power budget: the sizing case is hibernation at 1.468 au, 919 W at 630 W/m2; 180 W at a regulated 28 V go to the payload in the science phase (§5.5.2).
Link and storage budgets: 150 kbit/s at 1 au via the HGA to Malargüe; in-situ instruments produce data continuously, remote-sensing instruments during three 10-day windows per orbit (§5.5.3-5.5.4).
Solar flux reaches up to 12.7 Earth solar constants at perihelion; the solar array is tilted about its longitudinal axis to keep cell temperature manageable (§5.6).
For thermal reasons the HTHGA may have to be folded several times during the mission; maximum flux 17424 W/m2 at 0.28 au, minimum 784 W/m2 at 1.32 au (§5.6, §5.7).
Ground stations: ESA deep-space antennas at New Norcia, Cebreros and Malargüe; in the nominal phase Malargüe takes daily 9-hour passes, 8 hours of which are for science telemetry (§7.1.1).
An encounter typically consists of a 10-day window centred on perihelion and two 10-day windows centred on the highest latitudes (§7.2.3).
